explanations.explanation: Close, but the rule doesn't run on one witness. Paul quotes it like this: “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” One voice can be mistaken, so the rule asks for more than one. I'd be nervous if my whole case rested on one guy saying, "Trust me, I saw it."

Right, it takes more than one. Paul says, “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” The rule comes from Deuteronomy 19:15, and he brings it up right as he's about to visit. Two or three witnesses is a sturdy table, and one witness is a table with one wobbly leg.

That's the opposite of what Paul writes. He warns “those who sinned earlier and everyone else,” and then says, “If I return, I will not spare anyone.” Nobody gets a pass, and nobody gets singled out either. I think anyone reading that line sits up a little straighter.

Yes, no exceptions. Paul warns “those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone.” He says it to the ones who sinned and to everybody else. That's a warning aimed at the whole room, so nobody can pretend it was meant for the person sitting next to them.

explanations.answer: That Christ is speaking through Paul
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says they are “demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me.” Then he adds that Christ “is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you.” They asked for proof, and he points them to Christ.

explanations.answer: That Paul learned from Peter in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That one's not in these verses. Peter was one of Jesus' apostles (Matthew 10:2), but Paul never mentions him here. What the Corinthians are demanding is “proof that Christ is speaking through me.” It's a bit like asking for a recipe's source when the real question is whether the cookies are any good.

explanations.answer: That Paul was trained under Gamaliel
explanations.explanation: Gamaliel was a teacher in Jerusalem, and Paul does mention being brought up at his feet in Acts 22:3. But it isn't what the Corinthians are asking about here. Paul says they are “demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me.” A fancy teacher's name on the wall wasn't what they were after.

Yes, that's the first blank. Paul writes, “For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power.” The cross looked like weakness, and Paul says it plainly. I like that he doesn't dress it up.

That's the second blank, and it's a good one. “He lives by God’s power.” The same sentence that says weakness says power, and that's what Paul wants them to hear. Christ is not weak in dealing with them, and the very next verse says Paul and his companions will live with Him by that power too.

Not this one, friend. Paul doesn't say anything was done in secret here. He says Christ “was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power.” Nothing hidden in that sentence, just a plain statement said out loud.

Anger doesn't show up in this sentence. Paul writes that Christ “was indeed crucified in weakness.” He doesn't name a feeling there, so I wouldn't add one. The word he picked is weakness, and the next blank gets power.

Silence is a fair guess, but it's not Paul's word. He says Christ “was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power.” Nothing in that sentence is about quiet. It's a sentence with two big words, and neither one is whispering.

explanations.answer: Whether they are in the faith
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Paul says, “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves.” They had been demanding proof from him, and now he turns the question back to them. Funny how the clipboard changes hands.

That's pointing the clipboard the wrong way, friend. Paul tells them to “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith.” The check is about themselves, not about their leaders. It's a lot easier to inspect somebody else's oven than your own.

Gifts aren't what Paul has in mind here. He says, “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves.” The thing being tested is whether they are in the faith. It's the one question on the whole test.

explanations.answer: Paul's group appears to have failed
explanations.explanation: Yes, and that's a generous prayer. Paul says they pray “that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.” He'd rather the Corinthians do right than have his group look good. I'd take looking bad over a ruined batch any day, and Paul seems to agree.

explanations.answer: Paul's group never hears about it
explanations.explanation: Hearing about it isn't the point here. Paul says he wants them to “do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.” His group's reputation is what he's willing to give up. He isn't asking for good news to reach him.

explanations.answer: Paul's group never gets to visit
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul does talk about coming to them, but this verse isn't about visiting. He prays “that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.” What he's willing to risk is how his group looks.

That's the word, baker. Paul writes, “we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong.” He's glad to look small if the Corinthians are standing tall. That's a leader cheering from the back of the room, and I love it.

Humble sounds nice, but it's not the word Paul uses. He says, “we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong.” The contrast is weak and strong. Paul takes the weak seat and cheers for the strong ones.

Quiet doesn't fit this sentence. Paul says, “we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong.” He wants strength for the Corinthians, not silence. A strong church is probably a lot of things, but Paul never says quiet.

Yes, baker. Paul says the Lord gave him authority “for building you up, not for tearing you down.” That's the whole job description. A tool made for building doesn't do much good when it's swung like a wrecking ball.

Nope, that's not on the list. Paul says the authority is “for building you up, not for tearing you down,” and he means the Corinthians. The other apostles don't come up in this verse at all. He's talking about what the authority is for, and it's building.

explanations.answer: To collect the gift for Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: A good guess, but this verse says something else. Paul says the Lord gave him authority “for building you up, not for tearing you down.” No collection is mentioned in this verse. The purpose is building up.

explanations.answer: Aim for perfect harmony and live in peace
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul says, “Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace.” Four short things in a row, easy to remember and hard to do. Anybody who's tried to get a whole group to agree on one thing knows that harmony takes aim.

explanations.answer: Keep away from anyone who sinned before
explanations.explanation: That's not on Paul's list. He says, “Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace.” Nothing about staying away from anybody. The list is about living together.

explanations.answer: Stay quiet and wait until Paul arrives
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't ask for that here. His list is “Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace.” He gives them things to do, and waiting quietly isn't one of them. Encouraging one another takes some actual talking.

Yes, it's true, baker. Right after the list, Paul says, “And the God of love and peace will be with you.” He tells them what to do, and then he tells them who will be with them. That's a good way to send somebody off.
It's actually true. Paul ends the list with “And the God of love and peace will be with you.” He doesn't leave them with only instructions. After the warnings, that line is a warm one.

explanations.answer: The fellowship of the Holy Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul closes with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.” Father, Son and Holy Spirit are all named in one line. What a way to end a letter.

Close in sound, but not in the text. Paul's last line names “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.” The apostles aren't mentioned there. The three gifts are named after Jesus, God and the Holy Spirit.

The saints do appear a verse earlier, sending greetings, but they're not in this last line. Paul closes with “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.” The third one is the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Easy to mix up when the whole ending is one big warm sentence.
Not quite, friend. Paul ends with “be with all of you.” He doesn't draw a line between who has repented and who hasn't. After all those warnings, the last words are for everybody.

Right, it's for everyone. Paul closes with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.” The words are all of you. I'd say that's a pretty big blessing to end on.
